dct_description_sm: Light is one of the most important factors to determine the beginning of the algal growth. Important variations of light conditions are observed in sea ice during spring, from important snow pack conditions (low light) to the formation of meltponds (high light). Thus sea ice microalgae possess high photosynthetic plasticity to acclimate and protect themselves. However, Petrou et al. (2011) showed that the plasticity and photoacclimation of Antarctic diatoms depend of their niche habitats. Thus ice algae in the bottom sea ice and sinking could possess different capacities of photoacclimation. In addition, in the last few years, under-ice blooms have been increasingly observed at the end of spring, when light penetrating through the ice is sufficient to support algal growth. These under-ice blooms can be composed of different algal communities: phytoplanktonic centric diatoms vs sympagic pennate diatoms as observed in Resolute Passage by Galindo et al. (2014). Previous studies in Antarctic showed that the sympagic pennate diatoms have higher photoprotection capacities, but no study compared the plasticity of both communities (ice algae vs phytoplankton) at the same time. Because of the actual retreat and thinning of sea ice, it becomes essential to understand the photoprotection mechanisms of both algal communities.  This project aims to characterize the evolution of photoprotection and photoinhibition by ice algae during the ice algal bloom and compare the photoprotective capacities of bottom sea ice algae, sinking algae and phytoplankton.
dct_title_s: Photosynthetic and photoprotective properties of ice algae, phytoplankton and sinking algae at Qikiqtarjuak
